title: How to Analyze Time & Space Complexity
oneLiner: Big O tells you what O(n²) means; this is the skill of looking at actual code and working out which one it is.
keyTakeaway: Complexity is two questions multiplied together: (1) how many times does the loop or recursion run -- decided by the code's STRUCTURE -- and (2) what does each trip through it cost -- decided by which data-structure operations you call inside. The same loop is O(n) or O(n²) depending only on whether the thing inside it is a hash lookup or a list scan.
explanation:
The Big O lesson gives you a vocabulary and a lookup table. Neither helps much when someone hands you twelve lines of code and asks "what's the complexity?" -- that's a separate skill, and it comes down to a short procedure you can run on any snippet.

Step 1 -- count how many times the work repeats, from the code's shape alone. A single loop over n items runs n times. A loop nested in another loop over n runs n x n times. A loop that cuts its remaining range in half every trip (binary search, or `while (n > 1) n /= 2`) runs log n times. Two loops one AFTER the other add (n + n is still O(n)); loops one INSIDE the other multiply. A recursive function that calls itself twice per call roughly doubles at every level -- that's exponential, unless memoization (remembering the result of each call so a repeat is just a lookup) collapses the repeats.

Step 2 -- price each trip. This is where the data-structure cost table earns its keep: indexing an array is O(1), a hash-set lookup is O(1) on average, scanning a list with Contains is O(n), sorting is O(n log n), a heap push or pop is O(log n). Multiply Step 1 by Step 2. A loop over n items that calls `list.Contains(x)` inside is n x n = O(n²); the identical loop calling `set.Contains(x)` is n x 1 = O(n). That one swap is the entire reason a hash map turns Two Sum from O(n²) into O(n).

Step 3 -- keep only the biggest term and drop constants: n² + n becomes n², and 3n becomes n. Space works the same way, but you count what you ALLOCATE rather than what you repeat: a new array or hash set that grows with the input is O(n), and recursion costs one stack frame per level of depth, so a recursion n levels deep is O(n) space even if it allocates nothing else. Variables that don't grow with the input are O(1).
